A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JAM-Flow and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained experiments and illustrations can be matched despite substantial rewriting and reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark and ablation results in Tables 1–4 and a 26-participant user study in Appendix A.2.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark, ablation, and user-study results and adds a Stage-1 comparison, transcript audit, and source-separation experiment.

M1.justification: The specified Stage-1 procedure changes substantially. v1 Section 4.6 trains Motion-DiT through joint attention with a frozen Audio-DiT, including audio-loss backpropagation into motion parameters. v2 Section 4.5 and Appendix A.3 instead pretrain Motion-DiT using concatenated wav2vec2 features and introduce joint attention in Stage 2. The final dual-stream architecture and core flow-matching losses remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use CelebV-Dub, HDTF, and LibriSpeech-PC test-clean for the same training and task coverage. The text-only, reference-audio, and motion-conditioned generation scenarios already appear in v1. Added data-quality diagnostics investigate retained speech/data coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Ours-Stage1 as a comparator, while Table 2 removes the Vocoder Rec. comparison. The named external talking-head, TTS, and dubbing comparator sets otherwise remain unchanged. Ours† is not wholly removed: its frozen-Audio-DiT WER survives in Appendix C.1.

E3.justification: v2 adds a Stage-1 checkpoint evaluation, an H100-class timing setting, manual inspection of all 213 CelebV-Dub test videos, and a controlled comparison of F5-TTS outputs before and after source separation. Retained evaluations preserve the benchmark metrics, 32 NFE, 20-second segmentation, and 26-participant study. Newly disclosed architecture and guidance settings do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The Stage-1 comparison adds evidence about joint training, and Appendix C.1 adds diagnostics of transcript errors and transcription damage from source separation. The existing joint-block, masking, and Audio-DiT finetuning ablations remain unchanged, as do the principal qualitative use cases and failure cases.

E5.justification: The same user-study plots retain their error bars. Neither version adds repeated-run counts, seeds, defined confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new transcript-error proportions are additional findings, not a change in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark scores, Table 4 results, and user-study outcomes are unchanged. New results include Stage-1 HDTF FID 18.372 and FVD 194.27, 19-second generation of a 20-second video on H100-class hardware, transcript-error counts of 45/213 and 72/213, and source-separation WER increasing from 2.43% to 2.63%. Table 2 loses ground-truth/vocoder values and Ours† SIM-o 0.63; Ours† WER 3.38% moves to Appendix C.1. The H100 timing uses different conditions from the retained 45-second A6000 result.

T1.justification: The flow-matching mathematics, keypoint transformation, and RoPE scaling remain substantively equivalent. The added total-loss and standard classifier-free-guidance equations make previously described mechanisms explicit; they do not introduce new theoretical assumptions, proofs, or substantive derivations.

C1.justification: v2 reframes the central novelty from the first joint architecture to the first inpainting-style joint training framework for speech and facial motion. It also introduces near-real-time synthesis as an explicit contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The underlying claim of flexible, mutually conditioned audio–motion generation remains.

C2.justification: v1 cautiously attributes TTS degradation to noisy training data; v2 argues more strongly that label noise is the primary bottleneck and imposes a WER floor, while adding discussion of WER versus perceptual quality. It also states that freezing Audio-DiT prevents learning a proper joint distribution and explicitly qualifies perfect articulation as impossible when fixed motion conflicts with target text. Most earlier limitations and qualitative interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands reproducibility information: mel-spectrogram settings, 24 kHz audio, 25 FPS motion, transformer width and heads, modality-dropout probabilities, and shared CFG scale 2. Reported training time changes from approximately one day for both stages to approximately one day per stage. Some metric-implementation attribution and the explicit promised CC-BY-NC model license disappear. Code/model release remains prospective, and the project-page address is unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially updates positioning against recent avatar generators and acknowledges concurrent joint audio-video systems including Veo 3, LTX-2, and Klear. Novelty is redirected toward inpainting-style joint supervision, replacing v1's broader absence-of-prior-joint-model framing. Distillation literature is also added as a future efficiency direction; these citations do not constitute new evaluated baselines.

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions, TTS discussion, ablation interpretations, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Motion-DiT and Audio-DiT descriptions are merged, existing qualitative material is redistributed, and the appendix is reorganized around experimental details, qualitative evaluation, and discussion. These changes substantially alter the narrative beyond adding scientific content.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different template with changed typography, text width, running headers, author layout, captions, and float placement. Table 1 gains timing and parameter-count columns plus a Stage-1 row; Table 2 is shortened and embedded beside text. The existing main figures and appendix illustrations are retained but resized and relocated.

improvement.justification: v2 improves reproducibility through Appendix A's concrete settings and strengthens the empirical discussion of data noise through Appendix C.1's transcript audit and source-separation control. These useful gains are tempered by omitted TTS reference values and licensing information, unspecified engineering behind the new H100 timing, and a stronger WER-floor interpretation than the added tests establish. The net improvement is limited but supported.
